title: Pauri 3, meaning: the carefree one
hookLine: some sing His power, some His gifts; the Giver keeps giving though receivers tire, and He blossoms free of care (Japji 3)

cards: A grandmother at a family dinner keeps putting food on your plate. You say you're full. She adds another roti.
You say really, I'm done. She's already bringing dessert. In the end you're the one who gives up; she never does.
And she seems happy the whole time, not anxious, not keeping count. Guru Nanak's third pauri ends with a picture a little like that, only vast: a Giver who never tires, and receivers who do.

teach.h: SOME SING POWER, SOME SING GIFTS.
teach.b: Here is the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. Some sing of His power, if they have the power. Some sing of His gifts, and know them as His sign.

Some sing of His virtues, His greatness and His deeds. Some sing of knowledge gained through hard study. Some sing that He shapes the body and then turns it back to dust; some, that He takes life away and gives it again.
Some, that He seems far away; some, that He watches face to face, always present.
Millions upon millions tell it, and the telling never runs out. Then the turn.
Dedaa de, laide thak paahi: the Giver keeps giving; the receivers grow tired of receiving. Through age after age, they go on eating. By His order, the One who orders sets the path.
And the last line: Nanak, He blossoms, free of care. The word is veparvaahu. Parvaah is worry, concern; ve means without.
Carefree. Not careless, as in not caring: the opposite of anxious.
The Giver doesn't give out of need, or to be thanked, or while keeping count. In the pauri's picture, giving is simply what the Giver is. And vigsai, blossoms, is a flower word: opening, delighted.
Notice what the pauri does with all those singers from yesterday. It doesn't pick a winner. Power, gifts, far, near: all sing of the same Giver, and none finishes.
Some readers find relief in that: no singer has to get the song exactly right, and in the pauri the gifts keep coming anyway.

how: Sikhs recite the third pauri each morning in Japji; its closing picture of the carefree Giver is often quoted in talks on gratitude and on giving without counting.

o: free of worry, the opposite of anxious
a gift that is given back in return

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

s: it means free of worry: the opposite of anxious, not the opposite of caring.
the pauri says receivers tire before the Giver does
the pauri picks one right way to sing
power, gifts, far, near: all sing of the same Giver, and none finishes.

games.q: the Giver keeps giving, age after age. who gets tired first?
games.why: the receivers grow tired of receiving; the Giver goes on, and blossoms, free of care.

practice: Count three gifts from today, small and ordinary: the first sip of something warm, a text from someone, the breath you take without trying.

Name each one quietly, without hurrying, and notice that you didn't make most of them; they arrived. If you pray, you can thank the Giver in a word, Waheguru; if you don't, just let yourself feel given to.

wordCard.voice: Veparvaahu. Free of care: the Giver keeps giving though some sing His power, some His gifts, and there's no end to the telling.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the last line of pauri 3: Nanak, He blossoms, free of care.

carryVoice: Your line: the giver never tires. The week behind you: sach, sochai soch, hukam, hukmee, haumai and gaavai ko. That's the week.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 3
